outcome_verbatim: gainful employment (part or full time employment in compensated, non-supportive settings)
source_locator: Results section 3, p. 182 ('In the entire sample, 32.9% were employed'); Table 1, p. 182, row 'Gainful employment'; outcome definition at section 2.2, pp. 181-182
conflict_note: Table 1 (p. 182) prints "Gainful employment 60 (20.6%)" for schizophrenia (n=80) and "23 (53.4%)" for bipolar disorder (n=48). 60/80 = 75.0% and 23/48 = 47.9%, so neither count reproduces its own percentage. The counts sum to 83 of 128 (64.8%) whereas the text (Results section 3, p. 182) states "In the entire sample, 32.9% were employed"; 32.9% is instead what the two printed percentages give (0.206*80 + 0.534*48 = 42.1, and 42.1/128 = 32.9%). The Discussion (p. 183) adds "66/80 of the SCZ patients were both unemployed and living dependently", which leaves at most 14 schizophrenia participants employed or living independently and contradicts both readings. The analysed n is given as 122 in the Abstract and 128 in the Results. No numerator can be recovered without back-calculating from a percentage, so none was recorded. Unresolved; blocked from every synthesis.
notes: Reported only as a percentage of the whole analysed sample; the numerator is unrecoverable. reported_percentage_base = 128 is the sample the Results section names, but the Abstract names 122 for the same analysis, so even the base is contested. paid_any is NOT identified: the construct excludes work in 'non-supportive settings', so supported and sheltered paid work are outside the numerator and are not separable from the not-employed group.

outcome_verbatim: gainful employment (defined as competitively obtained part- or full-time employment vs. not employed in a steady job or participating in supported employment)
source_locator: Table 1, p. 12 of the author manuscript (Schizophr Res 2018;197:150-155), row 'Employed', schizophrenia column (n=146); outcome definition at Methods, 'Everyday Functioning', p. 4
conflict_note: ADJUDICATED 12 August 2026: reverted from resolved to unresolved. The extractor's reconstruction (Table 1's percentage column shifted one row, evidenced by the printed pair being byte-identical to strassnig2017's residence pair) is the candidate resolution and stands as the author query, but it is an inference, not an authority. The conflict_status vocabulary requires 'resolved' to record on whose authority, and no author reply or authorship-group ruling exists. D12.3d has no exception for a contradiction an extractor believes is adjudicable by arithmetic, and creating one after seeing the data is what the review's sequencing exists to prevent. ORIGINAL EXTRACTOR NOTE: Table 1 prints "Employed  36 (27.8%)" for schizophrenia (n=146) and "46 (76.7%)" for bipolar disorder (n=87). Neither percentage reproduces its count: 36/146 = 24.7% and 46/87 = 52.9%, and those two values are exactly the percentages printed one row above, on "Residentially Independent". The percentage column of the two functioning rows is therefore shifted by one row, and the pair printed against Employed (27.8%, 76.7%) is byte-identical to the pair printed against "Residential independence" in strassnig2017 Table 1, where it matches nothing either. Sex and race in the same table are internally consistent (88/146 = 60.3%, 105/146 = 71.9%), so the counts, not the counts-and-percentages jointly, are the reliable column. RESOLVED in favour of the counts 36/146 and 46/87 because they reproduce two printed percentages exactly and no alternative count is printed anywhere. Resolution rests on extractor arithmetic only; no author was contacted. A residual anomaly is unresolved and is logged separately: the printed chi-square statistics (39.6 for employment, 64.1 for residence) do not reproduce from these counts (19.0 and 38.5) or from any other reading.
notes: paid_any is NOT identified for this arm: the construct explicitly excludes anyone 'participating in supported employment', and supported and sheltered paid workers are pooled with the not-employed, so zero paid work is not separable. Bounds 36 <= paid_any <= 146. n_female = 146 - 88 male (Table 1) and is exact arithmetic on printed counts, not a back-calculation from a percentage. mean_age 47.9 is age at the 20-year assessment; baseline age is not printed.

outcome_verbatim: Employment status was based on register-data on main source of income during last year of follow-up. In descriptive analyses, employment status was grouped into social benefits (unemployed/in supported employment), education, and competitive employment. [extracted category: 'In competitive employment']
source_locator: Table 2, p. 52, 'Primary source of income at follow-up', EOP column (n=198); construct definition at Methods section 2.3 Outcome measures, p. 49
notes: paid_any is NOT identified. The register variable classifies people 'in supported employment' together with the unemployed under 'social benefits', so zero paid work is not separable from positive paid work and D12.3 forbids deriving paid_any. Bounds 49 <= paid_any <= 155 of 198. Ascertainment is period prevalence over the last year of follow-up ('main source of income during last year of follow-up'), not point prevalence. followup_basis is 'unclear' rather than 'since_baseline' as a deliberate block. The measurement is taken at a single calendar census date (31 December 2021), so elapsed follow-up runs from 4.5 to 23.5 years and the 139 months recorded here is a cohort MEAN spanning the 5-year and the 10-year-plus landmark bands. Coding it 'since_baseline' would place the cohort in the 108+ band on the strength of an average, which is the error D12.3b exists to prevent; the vocabulary has no value for 'mean elapsed follow-up to a fixed calendar date', so the horizon-blocking value was chosen and the gap is logged in unresolved_queries.md. The mean is itself contested: Results section 3.2 (p. 51) says 11.1 years, Table 2 (p. 52) says 11.6; 11.6 was used. Mean age at follow-up was 27.4 years (range 18 to 41).
